rows.notes: The cited document is a global meta-analysis of 74 published papers (Section 2.1, 591 side-by-side comparisons) on deficit irrigation versus full irrigation in cotton; it reports no data of its own, so Q1 is 'no' and all other questions are 'no'. Beyond the Q1 rule: the study does not compare subsurface versus surface drip at all; its soil-texture subgroup (Fig. 6, Section 3.4/4.4) concerns deficit-irrigation effects on seed cotton yield and WP across fine/medium/coarse soils, and the explanation about clay content, aeration and sandy soils is cited from other work (Bollmann and Conrad, Tiedje, Du et al., Lu et al.), not established by the study.

The cited document is a meta-analysis of published studies, not a primary study, so Q1 is 'no' and all other questions are 'no'. The statement that drip irrigation wets a small part of the soil while keeping the rest dry, improving aeration and uptake of water and nutrients, appears in Section 4.2 of the Discussion as an explanation drawn from other sources (Bonachela et al., 2001; Kang et al., 2004); the meta-analysis itself only reports pooled effect sizes showing that under deficit irrigation the yield reduction with drip (<U+2212>19.5%) was similar to furrow (<U+2212>19.6%) and smaller than sprinkler (<U+2212>36.2%) (Fig. 3a), with no significant WP difference among methods (Fig. 3b), and measures no aeration or uptake variables.

notes: Study is a global meta-analysis (74 papers, 15 countries) of deficit irrigation effects on seed cotton yield and water productivity; no original experimental data. Both claim rows therefore fail Q1. Full text appears complete.
